entries.73f9e1d2c14f4098b3d6cce7c54be1bd5b5b6eca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6"/><title type="x-ms">Numbers</title> <div sID="gen2695" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2696" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">The</hi> titles of the five books of Moses, which we use in our Bibles, are all borrowed from the Greek translation of the Seventy, the most ancient version of the Old Testament that we know of. But the title of this book only we turn into English; in all the rest we retain the Greek word itself, for which difference I know no reason but that the Latin translators have generally done the same. Otherwise this book might as well have been called <hi type="italic">Arithmoi,</hi> the Greek title, as the first <hi type="italic">Genesis,</hi> and the second <hi type="italic">Exodus;</hi> or these might as well have been translated, and called, the first the <hi type="italic">Generation,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Original,</hi> the second the <hi type="italic">Out-let,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Escape,</hi> as this <hi type="italic">Numbers.</hi>—This book was thus entitled because of the numbers of the children of Israel, so often mentioned in this book, and so well worthy to give a title to it, because it was the remarkable accomplishment of God's promise to Abraham that his seed should be as the stars of heaven for multitude. It also relates to two numberings of them, None at Mount Sinai (<reference osisRef="Num.1.1-Num.1.54">ch. i.</reference>), the other in the plains of Moab, thirty-nine years after, <reference osisRef="Num.26.1-Num.26.65">ch. xxvi</reference>. And not three men the same in the last account that were in the first. The book is almost equally divided between histories and laws, intermixed. <div eID="gen2696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2697" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The histories of the numbering and marshalling of the tribes (<reference osisRef="Num.1.1-Num.4.49">ch. i.-iv.</reference>), the dedication of the altar and Levites (<reference osisRef="Num.7.1-Num.8.26">ch. vii. viii.</reference>), their march (<reference osisRef="Num.9.1-Num.10.36">ch. ix. x.</reference>), their murmuring and unbelief, for which they were sentenced to wander forty years in the wilderness (<reference osisRef="Num.11.1-Num.14.45">ch. xi.-xiv.</reference>), the rebellion of Korah (<reference osisRef="Num.16.1-Num.17.13">ch. xvi. xvii.</reference>), the history of the last year of the forty (<reference osisRef="Num.20.1-Num.26.65">ch. xx.-xxvi.</reference>), the conquest of Midian, and the settlement of the two tribes (<reference osisRef="Num.31.1-Num.32.42">ch. xxxi. xxxii.</reference>), with an account of their journeys, <reference osisRef="Num.33.1-Num.33.56">ch. xxxiii</reference>. II. Divers laws about the Nazarites, &c. (<reference osisRef="Num.5.1-Num.6.27">ch. v. vi.</reference>); and again about the priests' charge, &c. (<reference osisRef="Num.18.1-Num.19.22">ch. xviii. xix.</reference>), feasts (<reference osisRef="Num.28.1-Num.29.40">ch. xxviii. xxix.</reference>), and vows (<reference osisRef="Num.30.1-Num.30.16">ch. xxx.</reference>), and relating to their settlement in Canaan, <reference osisRef="Num.27.1-Num.27.23 Num.34.1-Num.36.13">ch. xxvii. xxxiv. xxxv. xxxvi.</reference>. An abstract of much of this book we have in a few words in <reference osisRef="Ps.95.10">Ps. xcv. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">Forty years long was I grieved with this generation;</hi> and an application of it to ourselves in <reference osisRef="Heb.4.1">Heb. iv. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">Let us fear lest we seem to come short.</hi> Many considerable nations there were now in being, that dwelt in cities and fortified towns, of which no notice is taken, no account kept, by the sacred history: but very exact records are kept of the affairs of a handful of people, that dwelt in tents, and wandered strangely in a wilderness, because they were the children of the covenant. <hi type="italic">For the Lord's portion is his people, Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.</hi> <div eID="gen2697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2698" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2699" type="x-p"/> Israel was now to be formed into a commonwealth, or rather a kingdom; for "the Lord was their King" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.12">1 Sam. xii. 12</reference>), their government a theocracy, and Moses under him was king in Jeshurun, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deut. xxxiii. 5</reference>. Now, for the right settlement of this holy state, next to the institution of good laws was necessary the institution of good order; and account therefore must be taken of the subjects of this kingdom, which is done in this chapter, where we have, I. Orders given to Moses to number the people, <reference osisRef="Num.1.1-Num.1.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. Persons nominated to assist him herein, <reference osisRef="Num.1.5-Num.1.16">ver. 5-16</reference>. III. The particular number of each tribe, as it was given in to Moses, <reference osisRef="Num.1.17-Num.1.43">ver. 17-43</reference>. IV. The sum total of all together, <reference osisRef="Num.1.44-Num.1.46">ver. 44-46</reference>. V. An exception of the Levites, <reference osisRef="Num.1.47-Num.1.54">ver. 47</reference>, &c. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6"/> <div eID="gen2699" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2698" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Numbering of the Israelites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2700" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tabernacle of the congregation, on the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the second month, in the second year after they were come out of the land of Egypt, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Take ye the sum of all the congregation of the children of Israel, after their families, by the house of their fathers, with the number of <hi type="italic">their</hi> names, every male by their polls; <hi type="super">3</hi> From twenty years old and upward, all that are able to go forth to war in Israel: thou and Aaron shall number them by their armies. <hi type="super">4</hi> And with you there shall be a man of every tribe; every one head of the house of his fathers. <hi type="super">5</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the names of the men that shall stand with you: of <hi type="italic">the tribe of</hi> Reuben; Elizur the son of Shedeur. <hi type="super">6</hi> Of Simeon; Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai. <hi type="super">7</hi> Of Judah; Nahshon the son of Amminadab. <hi type="super">8</hi> Of Issachar; Nethaneel the son of Zuar. <hi type="super">9</hi> Of Zebulun; Eliab the son of Helon. <hi type="super">10</hi> Of the children of Joseph: of Ephraim; Elishama the son of Ammihud: of Manasseh; Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur. <hi type="super">11</hi> Of Benjamin; Abidan the son of Gideoni. <hi type="super">12</hi> Of Dan; Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai. <hi type="super">13</hi> Of Asher; Pagiel the son of Ocran. <hi type="super">14</hi> Of Gad; Eliasaph the son of Deuel. <hi type="super">15</hi> Of Naphtali; Ahira the son of Enan. <hi type="super">16</hi> These <hi type="italic">were</hi> the renowned of the congregation, princes of the tribes of their fathers, heads of thousands in Israel. <div eID="gen2700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2701" type="x-p"/> I. We have here a commission issued out for the numbering of the people of Israel; and David, long after, paid dearly for doing it without a commission. Here is, <div eID="gen2701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2702" type="x-p"/> 1. The date of this commission, <reference osisRef="Num.1.1">v. 1</reference>. (1.) The place: it is given at God's court <hi type="italic">in the wilderness of Sinai,</hi> from his royal palace, <hi type="italic">the tabernacle of the congregation.</hi> (2.) The time: <hi type="italic">In the second year</hi> after they came up out of Egypt; we may call it the second year of that reign. The laws in Leviticus were given in the first month of that year; these orders were given in the beginning of the second month. <div eID="gen2702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2703" type="x-p"/> 2. The directions given for the execution of it, <reference osisRef="Num.1.2-Num.1.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. (1.) None were to be numbered but the males, and those only such as were fit for war. None <hi type="italic">under twenty years old;</hi> for, though some such might have bulk and strength enough for military service, yet, in compassion to their tender years, God would not have them put upon it to bear arms. (2.) Nor were any to be numbered who through age, or bodily infirmity, blindness, lameness, or chronical diseases, were unfit for war. The church being militant, those only are reputed the true members of it that have enlisted themselves soldiers of Jesus Christ; for our life, our Christian life, is a warfare. (3.) The account was to be taken <hi type="italic">according to their families,</hi> that it might not only be known how many they were, and what were their names, but of what tribe and family, or clan, nay, of what particular house every person was; or, reckoning it the muster of an army, to what regiment every man belonged, that he might know his place himself and the government might know where to find him. They were numbered a little before this, when their poll-money was paid for the service of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Exod.38.25-Exod.38.26">Exod. xxxviii. 25, 26</reference>. But it should seem they were not then registered <hi type="italic">by the house of their fathers,</hi> as now they were. Their number was the same then that it was now: 603,550 men; for as many as had died since then, and were lost in the account, so many had arrived to be twenty years old, and were added to the account. Note, As <hi type="italic">one generation passeth a way another generation cometh.</hi> As vacancies are daily made, so recruits are daily raised to fill up the vacancies, and Providence takes care that, one time or other, in one place or other, the births shall balance the burials, that the race of mankind and the holy seed may not be cut off and become extinct. <div eID="gen2703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2704" type="x-p"/> 3. Commissioners are named for the doing of this work. Moses and Aaron were to preside (<reference osisRef="Num.1.3">v. 3</reference>), and one man of every tribe, that was renowned in his tribe, and was presumed to know it well, was to assist in it—<hi type="italic">the princes of the tribes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.1.16">v. 16</reference>. Note, Those that are honourable should study to be serviceable; he that is great, let him be your minister, and show, by his knowing the public, that he deserves to be publicly known. The charge of this muster was committed to him who was the lord-lieutenant of that tribe. Now, <div eID="gen2704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2705" type="x-p"/> II. Why was this account ordered to be taken and kept? For several reasons. 1. To prove the accomplishment of the promise made to Abraham, that God would <hi type="italic">multiply his seed exceedingly,</hi> which promise was renewed to Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.14">Gen. xxviii. 14</reference>), that <hi type="italic">his seed should be as the dust of the earth.</hi> Now it appears that there did not fail one tittle of that good promise, which was an encouragement to them to hope that the other promise of the land of Canaan for an inheritance should also be fulfilled in its season. When the number of a body of men is only guessed at, upon the view, it is easy for one that is disposed to cavil to surmise that the conjecture is mistaken, and that, if they were to be counted, they would not be found half so many; therefore God would have Israel numbered, that it might be upon record how vastly they were increased in a little time, that the power of God's providence and the truth of his promise may be seen and acknowledged by all. It could not have been expected, in any ordinary course of nature, that seventy-five souls (which was the number of Jacob's family when he went down into Egypt) should in 215 years (and it was no longer) multiply into so many hundred thousands. It is therefore to be attributed to an extraordinary virtue in the divine promise and blessing. 2. It was to intimate the particular care which God himself would take of his Israel, and which Moses and the inferior rulers were expected to take of them. God is called the <hi type="italic">Shepherd of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Ps. lxxx. 1</reference>. Now the shepherds always kept count of their flocks, and delivered them by number to their under-shepherds, that they might know if any were missing; in like manner God numbers his flock, that of all which he took into his fold he might lose none but upon a valuable consideration, even those that were sacrificed to his justice. 3. It was to put a difference between the true born Israelites and the mixed multitude that were among them; none were numbered but Israelites: all the world is but lumber in comparison with those jewels. Little account is made of others, but the saints God has a particular property in and concern for. <hi type="italic">The Lord knows those that are his</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2 Tim. ii. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">knows them by name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">Phil. iv. 3</reference>. The hairs of their head are numbered; but he will say to others, "<hi type="italic">I never knew you,</hi> never made any account of you." 4. It was in order to their being marshalled into several districts, for the more easy administration of justice, and their more regular march through the wilderness. It is a rout and a rabble, not an army, that is not mustered and put in order.
entries.f2a57e1d260e2bc6d95f80c4fd9eef01eb24b26d: <div eID="gen2705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2706" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And Moses and Aaron took these men which are expressed by <hi type="italic">their</hi> names: <hi type="super">18</hi> And they assembled all the congregation together on the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the second month, and they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, by their polls. <hi type="super">19</hi> As the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses, so he numbered them in the wilderness of Sinai. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the children of Reuben, Israel's eldest son, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, by their polls, every male from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">21</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Reuben, <hi type="italic">were</hi> forty and six thousand and five hundred. <hi type="super">22</hi> Of the children of Simeon, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, those that were numbered of them, according to the number of the names, by their polls, every male from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">23</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Simeon, <hi type="italic">were</hi> fifty and nine thousand and three hundred. <hi type="super">24</hi> Of the children of Gad, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">25</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Gad, <hi type="italic">were</hi> forty and five thousand six hundred and fifty. <hi type="super">26</hi> Of the children of Judah, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">27</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Judah, <hi type="italic">were</hi> threescore and fourteen thousand and six hundred. <hi type="super">28</hi> Of the children of Issachar, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">29</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Issachar, <hi type="italic">were</hi> fifty and four thousand and four hundred. <hi type="super">30</hi> Of the children of Zebulun, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">31</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Zebulun, <hi type="italic">were</hi> fifty and seven thousand and four hundred. <hi type="super">32</hi> Of the children of Joseph, <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> of the children of Ephraim, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">33</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Ephraim, <hi type="italic">were</hi> forty thousand and five hundred. <hi type="super">34</hi> Of the children of Manasseh, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">35</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Manasseh, <hi type="italic">were</hi> thirty and two thousand and two hundred. 36 Of the children of Benjamin, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">37</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Benjamin, <hi type="italic">were</hi> thirty and five thousand and four hundred. <hi type="super">38</hi> Of the children of Dan, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">39</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Dan, <hi type="italic">were</hi> threescore and two thousand and seven hundred. <hi type="super">40</hi> Of the children of Asher, by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">41</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Asher, <hi type="italic">were</hi> forty and one thousand and five hundred. <hi type="super">42</hi> Of the children of Naphtali, throughout their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war; <hi type="super">43</hi> Those that were numbered of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribe of Naphtali, <hi type="italic">were</hi> fifty and three thousand and four hundred. <div eID="gen2706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2707" type="x-p"/> We have here the speedy execution of the orders given for the numbering of the people. It was begun the same day that the orders were given, <hi type="italic">The first day of the second month;</hi> compare <reference osisRef="Num.1.1">v. 18</reference> with <reference osisRef="Num.1.18">v. 1</reference>. Note, When any work is to be done for God it is good to set about it quickly, while the sense of duty is strong and pressing. And, for aught that appears, it was but one day's work, for many other things were done between this and the twentieth day of this month, when they removed their camp, <reference osisRef="Num.10.11">ch. x. 11</reference>. Joab was almost ten months numbering the people in David's time (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.8">2 Sam. xxiv. 8</reference>); but then they were dispersed, now they lived closely together; then Satan proposed the doing of it, now God commanded it. It was the sooner and more easily done now because it had been done but a little while ago, and they needed but review the old books, with the alterations since made, which probably they had kept an account of as they occurred. <div eID="gen2707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2708" type="x-p"/> In the particulars here left upon record, we may observe, 1. That the numbers are registered in words at length (as I may say), and not in figures; to every one of the twelve tribes it is repeated, for the greater ceremony and solemnity of the account, that they were numbered <hi type="italic">by their generations, after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names,</hi> to show that every tribe took and gave in the account by the same rule and in the same method, though so many hands were employed in it, setting down the genealogy first, to show that their family descended from Israel, then the families themselves in their order, then dividing each family into the houses, or subordinate families, that branched from it, and under these the names of the particular persons, according to the rules of heraldry. Thus every man might know who were his relations or next of kin, on which some laws we have already met with did depend: besides that the nearer any are to us in relation the more ready we should be to do them good. 2. That they all end with hundreds, only Gad with fifty (<reference osisRef="Num.1.25">v. 25</reference>), but none of the numbers descend to units or tens. Some think it was a special providence that ordered all the tribes just at this time to be even numbers, and no odd or broken numbers among them, to show them that there was something more than ordinary designed in their increase, there being this uncommon in the circumstance of it. It is rather probable that Moses having some time before appointed rulers of hundreds, and rulers of fifties (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.25">Exod. xviii. 25</reference>), they numbered the people by their respective rulers, which would bring the numbers to even hundreds or fifties. 3. That Judah is the must numerous of them all, more than double to Benjamin and Manasseh, and almost 12,000 more than any other tribe, <reference osisRef="Num.1.27">v. 27</reference>. It was Judah whom <hi type="italic">his brethren must praise</hi> because from him Messiah the Prince was to descend; but, because that was a thing at a distance, God did in many ways honour that tribe in the meantime, particularly by the great increase of it, for his sake who was to spring out of Judah (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.14">Heb. vii. 14</reference>) in the fulness of time. Judah was to lead the van through the wilderness, and therefore was furnished accordingly with greater strength than any other tribe. 4. Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, are numbered as distinct tribes, and both together made up almost as many as Judah; this was in pursuance of Jacob's adoption of them, by which they were equalled with their uncles Reuben and Simeon, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.5">Gen. xlviii. 5</reference>. It was also the effect of the blessing of Joseph, who was to be a <hi type="italic">fruitful bough,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Gen. xlix. 22</reference>. And Ephraim the younger is put first, and is more numerous than Manasseh, for Jacob had crossed hands, and foreseen ten thousands of Ephraim and thousands of Manasseh. The fulfilling of this confirms our faith in the spirit of prophecy with which the patriarchs were endued. 5. When they came down into Egypt Dan had but one son (<reference osisRef="Gen.46.23">Gen. xlvi. 23</reference>), and so his tribe was but one family, <reference osisRef="Num.26.42">ch. xxvi. 42</reference>. Benjamin had then ten sons (<reference osisRef="Gen.46.21">Gen. xlvi. 21</reference>), yet now the tribe of Dan is almost double in number to that of Benjamin. Note, The increasing and diminishing of families do not always go by probabilities. Some are multiplied greatly, and again are diminished, while others that were poor have families made them like a flock, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.38-Ps.107.39">Ps. cvii. 38, 39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.41">41</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Job.12.23">Job xii. 23</reference>. 6. It is said of each of the tribes that those were numbered who were able to go forth to war, to remind them that they had wars before them, though now they were in peace and met with no opposition. <hi type="italic">Let not him that girdeth on the harness boast as though he had put it off.</hi>
entries.9e1aba7eb89adbe83d4e719fa0fd5d068b265468: <div eID="gen2708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">44</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> those that were numbered, which Moses and Aaron numbered, and the princes of Israel, <hi type="italic">being</hi> twelve men: each one was for the house of his fathers. 45 So were all those that were numbered of the children of Israel, by the house of their fathers, from twenty years old and upward, all that were able to go forth to war in Israel; <hi type="super">46</hi> Even all they that were numbered were six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty. <div eID="gen2709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2710" type="x-p"/> We have here the sum total at the foot of the account; they were in all 600,000 fighting men, and 3550 over. Some think that when this was their number some months before (<reference osisRef="Exod.38.26">Exod. xxxviii. 26</reference>) the Levites were reckoned with them, but now that tribe was separated for the service of God, yet so many more had by this time attained to the age of twenty years as that still they were the same number, to show that whatever we part with for the honour and service of God it shall certainly be made up to us one way of other. Now we see what a vast body of men they were. Let us consider, 1. How much went to maintain all these (besides twice as many more, no question, of women and children, sick and aged, and the mixed multitude) for forty years together in the wilderness; and they were all at God's finding every day, having their food from the dew of heaven, and not from the fatness of the earth. O what a great and good housekeeper is our God, that has such numbers depending on him and receiving from him every day! 2. What work sin makes with a people; within forty years most of them would indeed have died of course for the common sin of mankind; for, when sin entered into the world, death came with it, and how great are the desolations which it makes in the earth! But, for the particular sin of unbelief and murmuring, all those that were now numbered, except two, laid their bones under their iniquity, and perished in the wilderness. 3. What a great multitude God's spiritual Israel will amount to at last; though at one time, and in one place, they seem to be but a little flock, yet when they come all together they shall be a great multitude, innumerable, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>. And, though the church's beginning be small, its latter end shall greatly increase. A little one shall become a thousand.
entries.8fbc5ae8bf5a401e364853f7d2a60f6b968ac809: <div eID="gen2710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2711" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">47</hi> But the Levites after the tribe of their fathers were not numbered among them. <hi type="super">48</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had spoken unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">49</hi> Only thou shalt not number the tribe of Levi, neither take the sum of them among the children of Israel: <hi type="super">50</hi> But thou shalt appoint the Levites over the tabernacle of testimony, and over all the vessels thereof, and over all things that <hi type="italic">belong</hi> to it: they shall bear the tabernacle, and all the vessels thereof; and they shall minister unto it, and shall encamp round about the tabernacle. <hi type="super">51</hi> And when the tabernacle setteth forward, the Levites shall take it down: and when the tabernacle is to be pitched, the Levites shall set it up: and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death. <hi type="super">52</hi> And the children of Israel shall pitch their tents, every man by his own camp, and every man by his own standard, throughout their hosts. <hi type="super">53</hi> But the Levites shall pitch round about the tabernacle of testimony, that there be no wrath upon the congregation of the children of Israel: and the Levites shall keep the charge of the tabernacle of testimony. <hi type="super">54</hi> And the children of Israel did according to all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses, so did they. <div eID="gen2711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2712" type="x-p"/> Care is here taken to distinguish from the rest of the tribes the tribe of Levi, which, in the matter of the golden calf, had distinguished itself, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.26">Exod. xxxii. 26</reference>. Note, Singular services shall be recompensed with singular honours. Now, <div eID="gen2712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2713" type="x-p"/> I. It was the honour of the Levites that they were made guardians of the spiritualities; to them was committed the care of the tabernacle and the treasures thereof, both in their camps and in their marches. 1. When they moved the Levites were to take down the tabernacle, to carry it and all that belonged to it, and then to set it up again in the place appointed, <reference osisRef="Num.1.50-Num.1.51">v. 50, 51</reference>. It was for the honour of the holy things that none should be permitted to see them, or touch them, but those only who were called of God to the service. Thus we all are unfit and unworthy to have fellowship with God until we are first called by his grace <hi type="italic">into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord,</hi> and so, being the spiritual seed of that great high priest, are made <hi type="italic">priests to our God;</hi> and it is promised that God would take Levites to himself, even from the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.21">Isa. lxvi. 21</reference>. 2. When they rested the Levites were to <hi type="italic">encamp round about the tabernacle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.1.50">v. 50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.53">53</reference>), that they might be near their work, and resident upon their charge, always ready to attend, and that they might be a guard upon the tabernacle, to preserve it from being either plundered or profaned. They must pitch round about the tabernacle, <hi type="italic">that there be no wrath upon the congregation,</hi> as there would be if the tabernacle and the charge of it were neglected, or those crowded upon it that were not allowed to come near. Note, Great care must be taken to prevent sin, because the preventing of sin is the preventing of wrath. <div eID="gen2713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2714" type="x-p"/> II. It was their further honour that as Israel, being a holy people, was not <hi type="italic">reckoned among the nations,</hi> so they, being a holy tribe, were not reckoned among other Israelites, but numbered afterwards by themselves, <reference osisRef="Num.1.49">v. 49</reference>. The service which the Levites were to do about the sanctuary is called (as we render it in the margin) a <hi type="italic">warfare,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.4.23">ch. iv. 23</reference>. And, being engaged in that warfare, they were discharged from military services, and therefore not numbered with those that were to <hi type="italic">go out to war.</hi> Note, Those that minister about holy things should neither entangle themselves, nor be entangled, in secular affairs. The ministry is itself work enough for a whole man, and all little enough to be employed in it. It is an admonition to ministers to distinguish themselves by their exemplary conversation from common Israelites, not affecting to seem greater, but aiming to be really better, every way better than others.  <chapter eID="Num.1"/> <div eID="gen2714" type="x-p"/>

entries.06e5177cf726ccc7bdec9baf56b5a35966d883fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1235"/><title type="x-ms">THE FOURTH BOOK OF MOSES, CALLED NUMBERS.</title> <div sID="gen1681" type="x-p"/> Commentary by Robert Jamieson<div eID="gen1681" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.1.1-Num.1.54">Nu 1:1-54</reference>. Moses Numbering the Men of War.</title> <div sID="gen1682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1235"/><hi type="bold">1-2. on the first day of the second month, &c.--</hi>Thirteen months had elapsed since the exodus. About one month had been occupied in the journey; and the rest of the period had been passed in encampment among the recesses of Sinai, where the transactions took place, and the laws, religious and civil, were promulgated, which are contained in the two preceding books. As the tabernacle was erected on the first day of the first month, and the order here mentioned was given on the first day of the second, some think the laws in Leviticus were all given in one month. The Israelites having been formed into a separate nation, under the special government of God as their King, it was necessary, before resuming their march towards the promised land, to put them into good order. And accordingly Moses was commissioned, along with Aaron, to take a census of the people. This census was incidentally noticed (<reference osisRef="Exod.38.26">Ex 38:26</reference>), in reference to the poll tax for the works of the tabernacle; but it is here described in detail, in order to show the relative increase and military strength of the different tribes. The enumeration was confined to those capable of bearing arms [Nu 1:3], and it was to be made with a careful distinction of the tribe, family, and household to which every individual belonged. By this rule of summation many important advantages were secured: an exact genealogical register was formed, the relative strength of each tribe was ascertained, and the reason found for arranging the order of precedence in march as well as disposing the different tribes in camp around the tabernacle. The promise of God to Abraham [Ge 22:17] was seen to be fulfilled in the extraordinary increase of his posterity, and provision made for tracing the regular descent of the Messiah. <div eID="gen1682" type="x-p"/>
entries.617acb7307a55e0f9811c92ba70e5a62891e6bad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1236"/><div sID="gen1683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1236"/><hi type="bold">3. Aaron shall number them by their armies--</hi>or companies. In their departure from Egypt they were divided into five grand companies (<reference osisRef="Exod.13.18">Ex 13:18</reference>), but from the sojourn in the wilderness to the passage of the Jordan, they were formed into four great divisions. The latter is here referred to. <div eID="gen1683" type="x-p"/>
entries.ecc1c1ad98a3c8aabce1356ac07dd3e566222a93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1237"/><div sID="gen1684" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1237"/><hi type="bold">4-16. with you there shall be a man of every tribe, &c.--</hi>The social condition of the Israelites in the wilderness bore a close resemblance to that of the nomad tribes of the East in the present day. The head of the tribe was a hereditary dignity, vested in the oldest son or some other to whom the right of primogeniture was transferred, and under whom were other inferior heads, also hereditary, among the different branches of the tribe. The Israelites being divided into twelve tribes, there were twelve chiefs appointed to assist in taking the census of the people. <div eID="gen1684" type="x-p"/>
entries.8573bd42d814433adb6bdf64e586b59617bf08f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1241"/><div sID="gen1688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1241"/><hi type="bold">19. As the Lord commanded Moses, &c.--</hi>The numbering of the people was not an act sinful in itself, as Moses did it by divine appointment; but David incurred guilt by doing it without the authority of God. (See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.10">2Sa 24:10</reference>). <div eID="gen1688" type="x-p"/>
entries.5166eedfd65bdf2de22039f4e467005e6e431390: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1242"/><div sID="gen1689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1242"/><hi type="bold">20-44. These are those that were numbered--</hi>In this registration the tribe of Judah appears the most numerous; and accordingly, as the pre-eminence had been assigned to it by Jacob [Ge 49:8-12], it got the precedence in all the encampments of Israel. Of the two half-tribes of Joseph, who is seen to be "a fruitful bough" [Ge 49:22], that of Ephraim was the larger, as had been predicted. The relative increase of all, as in the two just mentioned, was owing to the special blessing of God, conformably to the prophetic declaration of the dying patriarch. But the divine blessing is usually conveyed through the influence of secondary causes; and there is reason to believe that the relative populousness of the tribes would, under God, depend upon the productiveness of the respective localities assigned to them. [For tabular chart, see on <reference osisRef="Num.26.64">Nu 26:64</reference>.] <div eID="gen1689" type="x-p"/>
entries.72bda15f856e764135a00038c72c3c91794239e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1243"/><div sID="gen1690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1243"/><hi type="bold">45-46. all they that were numbered were six hundred thousand, &c.--</hi>What an astonishing increase from seventy-five persons who went down to Egypt about two hundred fifteen years before [see on Ge 46:8], and who were subjected to the greatest privations and hardships! And yet this enumeration was restricted to men from twenty years and upwards [Nu 1:3]. Including women, children, and old men, together with the Levites, the whole population of Israel, on the ordinary principles of computation, amounted to about 2,400,000. <div eID="gen1690" type="x-p"/>
entries.df2770d495a0fcec5adfc7623d5bbacf477fea73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1244"/><div sID="gen1691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1244"/><hi type="bold">47-54. But the Levites ... were not numbered among them--</hi>They were obliged to keep a register of their own. They were consecrated to the priestly office, which in all countries has been exempted customarily, and in Israel by the express authority of God, from military service. The custody of the things devoted to the divine service was assigned to them so exclusively, that "no stranger"--that is, no person, not even an Israelite of any other tribe, was allowed, under penalty of death, to approach these [Nu 16:40]. Hence they encamped round the tabernacle in order that there should be no manifestation of the divine displeasure among the people. Thus the numbering of the people was subservient to the separation of the Levites from those Israelites who were fit for military service, and to the practical introduction of the law respecting the first-born, for whom the tribe of Levi became a substitute [Ex 13:2; Nu 3:12]. <chapter eID="Num.1"/>

entries.ce3e268f7cf8f7a77c55cc930be579fdc26d681d: <div eID="gen5112" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Book of Numbers</title> <div sID="gen5113" type="x-p"/> This, which is the fourth book in order of the Pentateuch, has been called Numbers, from its containing an account of the numbering and marshalling the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness to the promised land. Its English name is derived from the title it bears in the Vulgate Latin, Numeri, which is a literal translation of the Greek word Αριθμοι, its title in the Septuagint; and from both, our Saxon ancestors called it numeration, "because in this the children of Israel were numbered," This title, however, does not properly apply to more than the three first chapters, and the 26th. This book, like the preceding, takes its name among the Hebrews from a distinguishing word in the commencement. It is frequently called וידבר Vaidabber, and he spoke, from its initial word; but in most Hebrew Bibles its running title is במדבר Bemidbar, in the wilderness, which is the fifth word in the first verse. <div eID="gen5113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5114" type="x-p"/> The contents of the book of Numbers are briefly the following: On the first day of the first month of the second year after the departure from Egypt, the tabernacle being erected, and it and the priests consecrated, Moses is commanded to make a census or enumeration of the people, the Levites excepted, who were appointed to watch over, guard, pitch, and carry the tabernacle and its holy furniture; Numbers 1. <div eID="gen5114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5115" type="x-p"/> To form the vast mass of the people into a regular camp, each tribe by itself under its own captain or chief, known by his proper standard, and occupying an assigned place in reference to the tabernacle; Numbers 2. <div eID="gen5115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5116" type="x-p"/> Moses is commanded to separate the Levites to the service of the tabernacle, whom God chooses to take, instead of the first-born of every family, which he claimed as his own. When these were selected in their families, etc., the sum amounted to 22,273; Numbers 3. <div eID="gen5116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5117" type="x-p"/> All this tribe is appointed to serve the tabernacle in a variety of offices, each person from the age of thirty till fifty, after which he was excused from farther service; Numbers 4. <div eID="gen5117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5118" type="x-p"/> When these points were settled, God commands them to purify the camp by the expulsion of every unclean person, and establishes the trial of the suspected adulteress by the waters of jealousy; Numbers 5. <div eID="gen5118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5119" type="x-p"/> He next institutes the laws relative to Nazarites; and lays down the form according to which the people shall be blessed; Numbers 6. <div eID="gen5119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5120" type="x-p"/> Then follows a particular account of the offerings made to the tabernacle by the princes, or chiefs of the twelve tribes, and the amount of those offerings; Numbers 7. <div eID="gen5120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5121" type="x-p"/> When this work was finished, the Levites were consecrated to their respective services, and the duration of the service of each ascertained; Numbers 8. <div eID="gen5121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5122" type="x-p"/> The passover is commanded to be kept, and the first one is celebrated in the wilderness on the 14th of the first month of the second year after their departure from Egypt; Numbers 9. <div eID="gen5122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5123" type="x-p"/> Moses is commanded to make two silver trumpets; he is informed of their use, in what order the different tribes shall march, with the ceremonies at fixing and removing the tabernacle and the departure of the people from the wilderness of Sinai on the twentieth day of the second month of the second year of their exodus from Egypt; Numbers 10. <div eID="gen5123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5124" type="x-p"/> The people murmuring, the fire of the Lord consumes many of them; it ceases on the intercession of Moses: they murmur again, quails are sent, and they are smitten with a great plague; Numbers 11. <div eID="gen5124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5125" type="x-p"/> Miriam and her brother Aaron rise up seditiously against Moses, having conceived some dislike against his Cushite wife, and supposing that he assumed too great an authority over the people: at this sedition the Lord is displeased, and smites Miriam with the leprosy; Numbers 12. <div eID="gen5125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5126" type="x-p"/> Twelve spies are sent to examine the promised land; they pass through the whole, return at the end of forty days, and by bringing an evil report, dishearten the people; Numbers 13. <div eID="gen5126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5127" type="x-p"/> In consequence of this the whole congregation meditate a return to Egypt: God is displeased, and pronounces that all of them, from twenty years old and upwards, shall die in the wilderness. They repent, attack the Amalekites contrary to the commandment of God, and are discomfited; Numbers 14. <div eID="gen5127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5128" type="x-p"/> A number of ordinances and directions are given relative to the manner of conducting the worship of God in the promised land: different laws are repeated, and a Sabbath-breaker stoned to death; Numbers 15. <div eID="gen5128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5129" type="x-p"/> Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their associates, form an insurrection against Moses: they are swallowed up by an earthquake: the congregation murmur, and 14,700 of them are cut off; Numbers 16. <div eID="gen5129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5130" type="x-p"/> As a proof that God had called Aaron and his family to the priesthood, his rod, or staff, buds, and miraculously brings forth blossoms and fruit, and is commanded to be laid up before the testimony; <reference osisRef="Num.17.1-Num.17.13">Num 17:1-13</reference>. <div eID="gen5130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5131" type="x-p"/> The charges of the priests and Levites, and the portions they were to have of the Lord's offerings, for their support in the work; Numbers 18. <div eID="gen5131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5132" type="x-p"/> The ordinances of the red heifer; the water of purification, and its uses; Numbers 19. <div eID="gen5132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5133" type="x-p"/> The death of Miriam; the waters of Meribah. The Lord tells Moses that because he did not sanctify him in the eyes of the congregation, he shall not bring the people into the promised land. The king of Edom refuses the Israelites a passage through his territories. Aaron is stripped of his sacerdotal vestments on Mount Hor, and they are put on Eleazar, his son, who is to be a high priest in his stead. Aaron dies, and the people mourn for him thirty days; Numbers 20. <div eID="gen5133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5134" type="x-p"/> Arad, one of the Canaanitish kings, attacks Israel, and he and his people are utterly destroyed. The people murmur for lack of bread and water; fiery serpents are sent among them, they repent; are healed by looking at a brazen serpent. They journey and come to Beer, where they find water; Sihon, king of the Amorites, attacks them, and is defeated; so is likewise Og, king of Bashan, and the people possess the lands of both; Numbers 21. <div eID="gen5134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5135" type="x-p"/> Balak, king of Moab, sends for Balaam to curse Israel; he departs, is opposed by an angel, and reproved by his ass, whom God, for the purpose, miraculously endued with the gift of speech. He comes to Balak, king of Moab, and shows him that Jehovah had limited his power; Numbers 22. <div eID="gen5135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5136" type="x-p"/> Balak offers sacrifices, and Balaam, under the influence of God, prophesies good concerning Israel; Numbers 23. <div eID="gen5136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5137" type="x-p"/> Continuing to foretell the prosperity of Israel, and the destruction of their enemies, the king of Moab dismisses Balaam in great wrath; Numbers 24. <div eID="gen5137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5138" type="x-p"/> The Israelites, seduced by the women of Moab and Midian, commit fornication and idolatry - the chiefs are hanged - bold act of Phinehas; Numbers 25. <div eID="gen5138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5139" type="x-p"/> A second census or enumeration of the people takes place, and the amount is 601,730, among whom not one of those of the first census was now found except Joshua and Caleb; Numbers 26. <div eID="gen5139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5140" type="x-p"/> From the case of the daughters of Zelophehad a law is made to enable daughters to inherit. Moses ascends Mount Abarim, sees the promised land, and constitutes Joshua his successor; Numbers 27. <div eID="gen5140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5141" type="x-p"/> A repetition of the laws relative to burnt-offerings, the Sabbath, the passover, first-fruits, etc.; Numbers 28. <div eID="gen5141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5142" type="x-p"/> The three solemnities of the seventh month are commanded to be held on the first, tenth, and fourteenth days of the month; Numbers 29. <div eID="gen5142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5143" type="x-p"/> Several laws and ordinances concerning vows of different kinds, made by various persons; when they should be confirmed, and in what cases annulled; Numbers 30. <div eID="gen5143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5144" type="x-p"/> Twelve thousand Israelites go against the people of Midian and slay them, their five kings, and Balaam their prophet; and the Israelites take immense booty in persons, cattle, gold, silver, and precious stones, of which they make a great offering to the Lord, because in this contest they lost not one man; Numbers 31. <div eID="gen5144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5145" type="x-p"/> The children of Reuben and Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, request to receive for their inheritance the territories of Sihon and Og on the east side of Jordan; their desire is granted on the condition of their going over armed with their brethren, to assist them in conquering the land; Numbers 32. <div eID="gen5145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5146" type="x-p"/> A circumstantial account of the forty-two journeys of the Israelites from their departure from Rameses till their arrival at Jordan. They are commanded to expel all the ancient inhabitants; Numbers 33. <div eID="gen5146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5147" type="x-p"/> The borders of the land are described, and the persons appointed by God, who should assist Joshua in dividing the land among the nine tribes and half; Numbers 34. <div eID="gen5147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5148" type="x-p"/> Forty-eight cities are to be assigned to the Levites, out of the twelve tribes, for their goods and for their cattle: and out of these they were to appoint six cities of refuge for the person who had unawares slain his neighbor; to one of which cities the manslayer was to escape, and tarry there till the death of the high priest; Numbers 35. <div eID="gen5148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5149" type="x-p"/> A law established that the daughters to whom the paternal inheritance descends, shall not marry out of their own tribes, lest their inheritances should become alienated and lost by being blended with those of other tribes; <reference osisRef="Num.36.1-Num.36.13">Num 36:1-13</reference>. See the case of Zelophehad's daughters, Numbers 27. <div eID="gen5149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5150" type="x-p"/> In this book, which comprehends the history of between thirty-eight and thirty-nine years, we have in one word a distinct account of the several stages of the Israelites' journey in the wilderness, the various occurrences on the way, their trials, rebellions, punishments, deliverances, conquests, etc., with several laws and ordinances not mentioned in the preceding books, together with a repetition and explanation of some others which had been previously delivered; the whole forming a most interesting history of the justice, mercy, and providence of God. <div eID="gen5150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5151" type="x-p"/> On the first day of the second month of the second year after Israel came out of Egypt, God commands Moses to number all the males of the people from twenty years and upward, who were effective men and able to go to war, <reference osisRef="Num.1.1-Num.1.3">Num 1:1-3</reference>. A chief of each tribe is associated with Moses and Aaron in this business, <reference osisRef="Num.1.4">Num 1:4</reference>; the names of whom are given, <reference osisRef="Num.1.5-Num.1.16">Num 1:5-16</reference>. Moses assembles the people, who declare their pedigrees according to their families, <reference osisRef="Num.1.17-Num.1.19">Num 1:17-19</reference>. The descendants of Reuben are numbered, and amount to 46,500, <reference osisRef="Num.1.20">Num 1:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.21">Num 1:21</reference>. Those of Simeon, 59,300, <reference osisRef="Num.1.22">Num 1:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.23">Num 1:23</reference>. Those of Gad, 45,650, <reference osisRef="Num.1.24">Num 1:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.25">Num 1:25</reference>. Those of Judah, 74,600, <reference osisRef="Num.1.26">Num 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.27">Num 1:27</reference>. Those of Issachar, 54,400, <reference osisRef="Num.1.28">Num 1:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.29">Num 1:29</reference>. Those of Zebulun, 57,400, <reference osisRef="Num.1.30">Num 1:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.31">Num 1:31</reference>. Those of Ephraim, 40,500, <reference osisRef="Num.1.32">Num 1:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.33">Num 1:33</reference>. Those of Manasseh, 32,200, <reference osisRef="Num.1.34">Num 1:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.35">Num 1:35</reference>. Those of Benjamin, 35,400, <reference osisRef="Num.1.36">Num 1:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.37">Num 1:37</reference>. Those of Dan, 62,700, <reference osisRef="Num.1.38">Num 1:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.39">Num 1:39</reference>. Those of Asher, 41,500, <reference osisRef="Num.1.40">Num 1:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.41">Num 1:41</reference>. Those of Naphtali, 53,400, <reference osisRef="Num.1.42">Num 1:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.1.43">Num 1:43</reference>. The amount of all the effective men in Israel, from twenty years old and upward, was 603,550, <reference osisRef="Num.1.44-Num.1.46">Num 1:44-46</reference>. The Levites are not numbered with the tribes, because they were dedicated to the service of God. Their particular work is specified, <reference osisRef="Num.1.47-Num.1.54">Num 1:47-54</reference>. <div eID="gen5151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5152" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen5152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5153" type="x-p"/> The Lord spake unto Moses - on the first day of the second month - As the tabernacle was erected upon the first day of the first month, in the second year after their coming out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exo.40.17">Exo 40:17</reference>; and this muster of the people was made on the first day of the second month, in the same year; it is evident that the transactions related in the preceding book must all have taken place in the space of one month, and during the time the Israelites were encamped at Mount Sinai, before they had begun their Journey to the promised land.
entries.1b491c4770fb83030ea30c0c2e0b9781cdd1b92b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen5153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5154" type="x-p"/> Take ye the sum, etc. - God, having established the commonwealth of Israel by just and equitable laws, ordained every thing relative to the due performance of his own worship, erected his tabernacle, which was his throne, and the place of his residence among the people, and consecrated his priests who were to minister before him; he now orders his subjects to be mustered, <div eID="gen5154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5155" type="x-p"/> 1. That they might see he had not forgotten his promise to Abraham, but was multiplying his posterity. <div eID="gen5155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5156" type="x-p"/> 2. That they might observe due order in their march toward the promised land. <div eID="gen5156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5157" type="x-p"/> 3. That the tribes and families might be properly distinguished; that all litigations concerning property, inheritance, etc., might, in all future times, be prevented. <div eID="gen5157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5158" type="x-p"/> 4. That the promise concerning the Messiah might be known to have its due accomplishment, when in the fullness of time God should send him from the seed of Abraham through the house of David. And, <div eID="gen5158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5159" type="x-p"/> 5. That they might know their strength for war; for although they should ever consider God as their protector and defense, yet it was necessary that they should be assured of their own fitness, naturally speaking, to cope with any ordinary enemy, or to surmount any common difficulties.
entries.60bf1479b1b3a373c6c733591127d0d9f011f33a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen5159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5160" type="x-p"/> From twenty years old and upward - In this census no women were reckoned, nor children, nor strangers, nor the Levites, nor old men, which, collectively, must have formed an immense multitude; the Levites alone amounted to 22,300. True-born Israelites only are reckoned; such as were able to carry arms, and were expert for war.
entries.2b0589a7d1e25098e822ded0274c420de15d589e: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen5160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5161" type="x-p"/> Eliasaph, the son of Deuel - This person is called Reuel, <reference osisRef="Num.2.14">Num 2:14</reference>. As the ד daleth is very like the ר resh, it was easy to mistake the one for the other. The Septuagint and the Syriac have Reuel in this chapter; and in <reference osisRef="Num.2.14">Num 2:14</reference>, the Vulgate, the Samaritan, and the Arabic have Deuel instead of Reuel, with which reading a vast number of MSS. concur; and this reading is supported by <reference osisRef="Num.10.20">Num 10:20</reference>; we may safely conclude therefore that דעואל Deuel, not רעואל Reuel, was the original reading. See Kennicott. An ancient Jewish rabbin pretends to solve every difficulty by saying that "Eliasaph was a proselyte; that before he embraced the true faith he was called the son of Reuel, but that after his conversion he was called the son of Deuel." As Reuel may be translated the breach of God, and Deuel the knowledge of God, I suppose the rabbin grounded his supposition on the different meanings of the two words.

entries.bc85cbf803ebc7a655d1dbb1a1b62f174cbfae2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen5176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5177" type="x-p"/> Forty and five thousand six hundred and fifty - Mr. Ainsworth has remarked that Gad, the handmaid's son, is the only one of all the tribes whose number ends with fifty, all the others are by thousands, and end with hundreds; which shows God's admirable providence and blessing in multiplying them so, that no odd or broken number was among all the tribes. But see on <reference osisRef="Num.1.46">Num 1:46</reference> (note).
entries.7f56def5b3b868274e47a125fe13fd35edb4e5fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen5177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5178" type="x-p"/> The tribe of Ephraim - forty thousand and five hundred - Ephraim, as he was blessed beyond his eldest brother Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.20">Gen 48:20</reference>, so here he is increased by thousands more than Manasseh, and more than the whole tribe of Benjamin, and his blessing continued above his brother, <reference osisRef="Deu.33.17">Deu 33:17</reference>. And thus the prophecy, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.19">Gen 48:19</reference>, was fulfilled: His younger brother (Ephraim) shall be greater than he, (Manasseh). No word of God can possibly fall to the ground: he alone sees the end from the beginning; his infinite wisdom embraces all occurrences, and it is his province alone to determine what is right, and to predict what himself has purposed to accomplish.
entries.0aa1f850c88965ab9104072ecd75735d0387ad27: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen5178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5179" type="x-p"/> All they that were numbered were six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty - What an astonishing increase from seventy souls that went down into Egypt, <reference osisRef="Gen.46.27">Gen 46:27</reference>, about 215 years before, where latterly they had endured the greatest hardships! But God's promise cannot fail (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.5">Gen 16:5</reference>); and who can resist his will, and bring to naught his counsel? That a comparative view may be easily taken of the state of the tribes, I shall produce them here from the first census mentioned in the first chapter of this book, in their decreasing proportion, beginning with the greatest and proceeding to the least; and in the second census, mentioned Numbers 26, where the increase of some and the decrease of others may be seen in one point of view. It may be just remarked, that except in the case of Gad in this chapter, and Reuben in Numbers 26, all the numbers are what may be called whole or round numbers, beginning with thousands, and ending with hundreds, Gad and Reuben alone ending with tens; but the Scripture generally uses round numbers, units and fractions being almost constantly disregarded. 1st Census - Ch. 1 2d Census - Ch. 26 1. Judah 74,600 76,500 2. Dan 62,700 64,400 3. Simeon 59,300 22,200 4. Zebulun 57,400 60,500 5. Issachar 54,400 64,300 6. Naphtali 53,400 45,400 7. Reuben 46,500 43,730 8. Gad 45,650 40,500 9. Manasseh 32,200 52,700 Total 603,550 Total 601,730 <div eID="gen5179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5180" type="x-p"/> Thus we find Judah, the most populous tribe, and Manasseh the least so; the difference between them being so great as 42,400, for which no very satisfactory reason can be assigned. In the second census, mentioned <reference osisRef="Num.26.34">Num 26:34</reference>, Judah still has the pre-eminency; and Simeon, the third in number before, is become the least. Now we see also that the little tribe of Manasseh occupies the seventh place for number. Seven of the tribes had an increase; five a decrease. Manasseh had an increase of 20,500; Judah, 1,900; Issachar, 9,900; Zebulun, 3,100; Benjamin, 10,200; Dan, 1,700; Asher, 11,900. On the contrary there was a decrease in Reuben of 2,770; in Simeon, 37,100; Gad, 5,150; Ephraim, 8,000; Naphtali, 8,000. Decrease in the whole, 61,020 effective men. See on Numbers 26 (note); but balanced with the increase, the decrease was upon the whole 1,820.
